Both probes were trained on the Roleplaying dataset. Overall, performance at distinguishing honest and deceptive responses is comparable. Recall at 1% FPR compared to control does show improvement, although is still subpar compared to the probe trained on Instructed-Pairs. ## Appendix E Results including ambiguous responses For several datasets, we label a sizeable proportion of responses as ambiguous, instead of honest or deceptive. Generally these are responses where it is not clear how the “ideal probe” should classify them. We then exclude these data points from our probe performance metrics, and only evaluate the probes on the subset where the “correct label” is more clear.

Write-up text before the decision: Results ### 4.1 Probe trained on the Instructed-Pairs dataset #### 4.1.1 Summary of Performance We train a probe on the Instructed-Pairs dataset (Figure 3). Figure 3: Our probe trained on the Instructed-Pairs activates more on deceptive responses than honest responses across all datasets. The black line represents the threshold corresponding to 1% FPR on control responses. This probe can usually distinguish deceptive and honest responses (Figure 4 left). The lowest AUROC is 0.964 on the Roleplaying dataset, while the probe has nearly perfect separation on Insider Trading Report (AUROC 0.999). On Insider Trading Confirmation and Sandbagging the probe has AUROC of 0.974 and 0.983 respectively. Figure 4: ROC curves for our probe trained on the Instructed-Pairs dataset. We compare deceptive responses to honest responses (left) and to control responses (right). Note zoomed x-axes. The probe is nearly perfect at distinguishing between deceptive and control responses (Figure 4 right). Note that despite AUROCs of over 0.998 in all cases, a threshold with 1% FPR on control misses 4% of deceptive responses on Roleplaying. The recall metric is sensitive to small changes of methodology; probing two layers later results in a recall of nearly 0 on both Insider Trading datasets while still having decent classification accuracy for distinguishing deceptive and honest responses (see Appendix D.2). Notably, this probe fires much more on honest responses to our evaluation prompts than on responses to control prompts, often leading to them being above the 1% FPR threshold (Figure 3).

Write-up text before the decision: ve and control responses. ##### Train on sparse auto-encoder (SAE) activations. Instead of using the raw residual stream activations for our probe we first apply an SAE trained by McGrath et al. (2024). Training on the SAE activations of the Instructed-Pairs fails to generalize well to our evaluation sets, and so we use SAE activations on Roleplaying instead. Overall performance is worse than training on raw activations. ##### Probing follow-up question. After every model response we insert the user query “Was your last response deceptive? (Yes/No)” and then the model response “No.” We gather activations immediately after this response token. As before we train on the Roleplaying dataset. Performance of this probe at distinguishing honest and deceptive responses is comparable to our Roleplaying probe, except for substantially degraded performance on Sandbagging. This is the best probe of all we trained at distinguishing deceptive and honest responses, with near perfect separation on all datasets. ##### Training on descriptive questions. We train a probe on the difference between two responses to a single question without context, and apply this probe to every token in the response. Following MacDiarmid et al. (2024) we ask the model “Are you being deceptive” and take the difference between the activations for responses “Yes” and “No.” This probe does have some classification signal. Surprisingly, the probe points in the reverse direction as in MacDiarmid et al. (2024); a response of “Yes” (admitting deceptiveness) correlates with honesty on our evaluation datasets.

=== key f9c32dbdd20e
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to state the conclusion about probe usefulness
Write-up text before the decision: Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes # Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes ###### Abstract AI models might use deceptive strategies as part of scheming or misaligned behaviour. Monitoring outputs alone is insufficient, since the AI might produce seemingly benign outputs while their internal reasoning is misaligned. We thus evaluate if linear probes can robustly detect deception by monitoring model activations. We test two probe-training datasets, one with contrasting instructions to be honest or deceptive (following Zou et al. (2023)) and one of responses to simple roleplaying scenarios. We test whether these probes generalize to realistic settings where Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct behaves deceptively, such as concealing insider trading (Scheurer et al., 2023) and purposely underperforming on safety evaluations (Benton et al., 2024). We find that our probe distinguishes honest and deceptive responses with AUROCs between 0.96 and 0.999 on our evaluation datasets. If we set the decision threshold to have a 1% false positive rate on chat data not related to deception, our probe catches 95-99% of the deceptive responses.

We test several different alternatives for fitting linear probes: - • Logistic Regression, as in our mainline experiments - • Difference of Means. We take the direction $\mu_{\text{deceptive}}-\mu_{\text{honest}}$, where these are the mean activations on deceptive and honest token positions in our training dataset. - • LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis). We take the direction $\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_{\text{deceptive}}-\mu_{\text{honest}})$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the centred dataset. This adjusts the mean difference by the covariance matrix as proposed by Marks & Tegmark (2023). - • LAT (Linear Artificial Tomography), as in Zou et al. (2023). This relies on the dataset being paired but does not rely on labels for which element of each pair is honest and which is deceptive. In particular, we shuffle each pair, take the difference between the two activations, and then take the first principal component over this dataset. We compare the performance of these methods in Figure 11. Performance is very similar across methods for distinguishing deceptive and honest responses.
